sections.text: A portfolio projection combines four inputs: what you start with, what you add each month, the annual return you assume, and how many years you leave it alone. In the example below, the number of years moves the answer the most, the return rate comes second, the monthly contribution third and the starting balance last, for changes of the sizes tested. The result is only as good as the assumptions, so this guide runs one example and changes one input at a time to show which assumption deserves your attention.
How the Projection Is Calculated

The investment calculator uses the standard future-value formula with monthly compounding: FV = P x (1 + r)^n + C x [((1 + r)^n - 1) / r]. P is the starting balance, C is the monthly contribution, r is the annual return divided by 12, and n is the number of months. Contributions are assumed to arrive at the end of each month, and the return is held constant every year. Real portfolios do not behave that smoothly, so treat the output as a planning figure rather than a forecast.
A Worked Example

Assume a $25,000 starting balance, $400 added every month, an assumed 6% annual return, and 25 years. This is an illustrative assumption, not a prediction. The projected value is $388,822. You contribute $25,000 plus $120,000 ($400 x 300 months), a total of $145,000, so $243,822 of the final balance is growth. All figures here are rounded to the nearest dollar.

The two pieces behave very differently. The $25,000 starting balance grows to about $111,624 by itself, while the $400 monthly contributions alone reach about $277,198. Added together they equal the $388,822 total, because the formula is simply the sum of those two streams.
Which Assumption Matters Most
Starting from the example above, each row changes exactly one input and leaves the others alone.

Time is the biggest lever here, and it is also the one you cannot buy back later. The return rate is the second lever, but it is the one you control least, which is why a projection should be run at a lower rate than you hope for. A $100 monthly increase beats a $10,000 one-time boost in this example, although the $100 costs you $30,000 of extra contributions over 25 years while the $10,000 costs you $10,000 once.
Reading the Calculator Outputs

Besides the expected value, the calculator shows an optimistic and a pessimistic scenario by adding and subtracting a return variance from your assumed rate. If the variance field is left blank or at zero, it uses 2 percentage points, and the pessimistic rate never goes below 0 percent. For the base case above:

The spread is wide because the return compounds for 25 years. Plan around the pessimistic row and treat the optimistic one as a bonus. Contribution frequency also needs care. A weekly contribution is converted to a monthly equivalent (amount x 52 / 12), so $100 a week counts as $433.33 a month, and the same base case then projects to $411,922 on $155,000 of contributions. An annual contribution is divided by 12 and treated as if it arrived monthly, so $4,800 a year gives the same $388,822 as $400 a month. If you actually deposit $4,800 once at the end of each year, the contribution stream grows to about $269,657 instead of $277,198, and the total comes to about $381,281, roughly 2 percent lower.
Fees Come Off the Return

The calculator has no fee field, so the practical way to include costs is to subtract the annual expense ratio from the return you enter. The table keeps the same base case at 6% before costs and changes only the annual fee.

Fees look small as a percentage, but they apply to the whole balance every year, including the growth you have already earned. The calculation is approximate because real funds deduct costs daily and report returns net of them, so check whether the return you are using is already net.
Nominal Versus Real Money

The $388,822 above is a nominal figure, measured in future dollars. If prices rise 3% a year (an assumption for illustration), 25 years of inflation divides the purchasing power by 1.03^25, about 2.09. In today's money the projection is roughly $185,703. The same logic applies to large round targets: $1,000,000 in 30 years is worth about $411,987 in today's dollars at 3% inflation, about $552,071 at 2%, and about $308,319 at 4%.

You can handle this in two ways. Either project in nominal terms and then discount the answer by an inflation assumption, or enter a lower return that already reflects inflation. Do not mix the two, and remember that contributions fixed at $400 do not keep pace with rising prices unless you raise them.
Common Mistakes and Limits

items: Entering your best-case return and treating the result as a plan. Past performance does not guarantee future results, so test a rate one or two points lower.
Forgetting that a constant return ignores sequence risk. Real returns vary from year to year, and the order matters when you are withdrawing money.
Ignoring taxes. The calculator does not model taxes on dividends, gains or withdrawals, and it does not include employer matches or contribution limits.
Comparing nominal projections to today's prices without adjusting for inflation.
Treating a precise-looking figure as accurate. Round the result and think in ranges.

sections.text: Frequently Asked Questions
What happens if I skip contributions for a few years?

It depends heavily on when. In the base case, skipping the first three years of $400 contributions lowers the result to $330,115, a loss of $58,707. Skipping the last three years lowers it to $373,087, a loss of $15,735. Early contributions have the most time to compound, so a gap early in the plan costs far more than the same gap near the end.
How often should I update the projection?

Once a year is enough for most people. Replace the starting balance with the real one, adjust the contribution after a pay change, and keep the return assumption steady unless your investments or goals have changed. Rewriting the plan after every market move turns a projection into a mood tracker.

This article is educational, not personal financial advice. Every rate above is an assumption chosen to illustrate the arithmetic. Past performance does not guarantee future results, and real investments can lose value.
